titulo: I Didn't Sleep for 7 Days (Cartoon Experiment)
descripcion:
Mokordo bet his friend he could stay awake for seven days straight. Here's what happens to the body, day by day: blue light and melatonin, sleep pressure, caffeine, junk food cravings, mood swings, microsleeps, hallucinations, the brain's night-shift cleaning crew... and how you recover.

This is a cartoon for education only. Don't try it: going without sleep is dangerous. If you can't sleep night after night, talk to a doctor.

🔔 Subscribe to Why Though for the why behind everyday things.
tags: what happens if you don't sleep

planos.narracion: This is Mokordo on day six without sleep.
Six days ago, he was totally fine. So what happened? Let's go back to the beginning.
Mokordo just made the dumbest bet of his life.
His friend Bob said nobody can stay awake for seven whole days. Mokordo said: watch me.
So for the next seven days: no naps, no bed, not even a blink that lasts too long.
And what happens to his body is wild. By day three, he'll be eating like a monster.
By day five, he'll be seeing things that aren't there.
And on day seven... well. You'll see.
Quick warning: this is a cartoon. Please don't try this at home. It's genuinely dangerous.
Day one. Eleven p.m. Bedtime. Mokordo puts on his pajamas... and grabs his phone instead.
One video. Then another one. Then a cat playing the piano.
That bright screen tricks his brain into thinking it's still daytime, so it holds back melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy.
Two a.m. His body starts to fight back.
Every hour you stay awake, a chemical called adenosine builds up in your brain. Scientists call it sleep pressure.
Normally, a night of sleep clears it away. Tonight, nobody is clearing anything.
Three a.m. He tries counting sheep to pass the time. Wait. No. That's the opposite of the plan.
To stay awake, he tries everything. Cold water on the face.
Jumping rope at three in the morning.
Video games, with the volume all the way up.
Six a.m. The alarm goes off. For everyone else, it's morning. For Mokordo, it's still yesterday.
Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep a night. Mokordo got zero.
And here's the trap: he feels... kind of okay. The first night, stress hormones keep you going.
Day two. Mokordo walks into work like an extra from a zombie movie.
Bob slept eight hours. Bob looks like a shampoo commercial.
After about seventeen hours awake, your reactions are as slow as someone who's had a couple of drinks.
After twenty four hours, it's like being over the legal limit for driving.
So Mokordo does what everybody does. Coffee.
Then a second coffee. Then a third one.
Here's the thing: caffeine doesn't give you energy. It just blocks the adenosine signal, like putting a pillow over a fire alarm.
The tiredness is all still there. He just can't hear it anymore.
Lunch break. He puts salt in his coffee instead of sugar. And drinks it anyway.
His password? Gone. His own phone number? Also gone.
And his heart is not a fan.
Then, in a meeting, his boss asks him a simple question... and his brain just leaves.
Sleep loss hits memory hard. After a night without sleep, people store about forty percent fewer new memories.
Mokordo has now read the same email eleven times.
Day three. Mokordo opens the fridge, and something wild wakes up inside him.
Without sleep, your hunger hormone, ghrelin, goes up. And leptin, the I'm full hormone, goes down.
And a tired brain wants junk. Sugar, fat, salt. All of it. Right now.
Two pizzas later, Mokordo can't see his own feet.
In studies, people who don't get enough sleep eat around three hundred and eighty extra calories a day.
Scientists even found that sleep loss boosts a chemical in the blood linked to the munchies, the same kind of craving cannabis gives you, especially in the afternoon and evening.
Mokordo steps on the scale. The scale would like to file a complaint.
Then his mood breaks too. The toaster burns his toast, and he completely loses it.
Five minutes later, he's crying at a dog food commercial.
That's real. The brain's emotional alarm, the amygdala, reacts about sixty percent more after a night without sleep.
And the part that keeps your emotions in check, right behind your forehead, goes quiet.
So on day three, everything is either a tragedy, or the funniest thing he's ever seen.
Day four. Mokordo goes for a walk to wake himself up.
Then, mid step, his brain switches off for a few seconds. A microsleep.
His eyes can even stay open during a microsleep. He's just... not there.
That's why drowsy driving is so dangerous. It plays a part in roughly one in six deadly crashes.
Good news: Mokordo isn't driving. He's sitting on a bench... and he's out cold in two seconds.
Bob asks him how he's feeling. He tries to say I'm fine. It comes out as: I'm fridge.
His reaction time is now about as fast as a turtle on vacation.
Bob is not having it. Splash!
And now things get weird. The trees look like they're breathing.
After a few days with no sleep, many people start to hallucinate: seeing shapes and hearing sounds that aren't there.
Mokordo is now having a deep conversation with a light bulb.
The light bulb is winning the argument.
Day five. Achoo!
His immune system is running on empty. People who sleep under six hours are about four times more likely to catch a cold.

planos.narracion: So Mokordo drags himself to the doctor.
His temperature is off, his hands are shaking, and his skin is breaking out.
The doctor tests his reflexes. Tap. Nothing. Tap. Nothing. Tap... oh, there it is.
Doctor: when did you last sleep? Mokordo: what day is it?
The doctor's face says it all.
Without deep sleep, your body can't repair itself properly. Muscles, skin, everything falls behind.
Blood pressure goes up. And after just a few short nights, healthy young people can test closer to pre diabetic.
At this point, Mokordo is held together by coffee and pure stubbornness.
Day six. Can a human even do this? Someone actually tried.
In nineteen sixty four, a seventeen year old student named Randy Gardner stayed awake for about eleven days. For a school science fair.
That's two hundred and sixty four hours. By the end, he could barely speak or remember things.
Today, record books won't even accept new attempts. It's considered too dangerous.
In lab experiments, rats kept awake for two or three weeks didn't survive.
And scientists found a big reason why. At night, your brain takes out the trash.
During deep sleep, the gaps between brain cells open up, and fluid rushes through to wash the waste away. Basically, a brain shower.
And deep sleep is also when your body releases most of its growth hormone. That's one reason babies and teenagers sleep so much.
While you sleep, your brain also files away what you learned today. No sleep, no saving. Like closing a game without hitting save.
Skip sleep, and the trash piles up. Even one night without sleep leaves more of a protein linked to Alzheimer's.
Mokordo's brain right now looks like a teenager's bedroom.
And with that, his body simply gives up.
Day seven. Mokordo loses the bet. He falls face first onto the bed.
And he sleeps. And sleeps. And sleeps.
Good news: you don't have to pay back every lost hour. Your body catches up by sleeping deeper, not longer.
Fourteen hours later, he wakes up, looks around, and asks: did I win?
After his record, Randy Gardner slept for about fourteen hours, and then went back to normal.

planos.narracion: The next morning, Mokordo looks in the mirror.
The dark circles are fading. His color is back. His brain feels clean again.
And Bob? Bob just wants his money.
Most of the short term damage from a week like this fades after a few good nights.
But years of sleeping too little are different. They're linked to heart disease, diabetes and memory problems.
So tonight, put the phone down an hour before bed.
Keep your room dark and cool, and wake up at the same time every day. Yes, even on weekends.
Easy on the coffee after lunch. Caffeine can stay in your body for many hours.
And get some sunlight in the morning. It tells your body clock when the day starts.
If you're a teenager, you need even more: eight to ten hours.
And if you really can't sleep, night after night, talk to a doctor. Insomnia is common, and it can be treated.
So tell me in the comments: how many hours did you sleep last night?
